I. The Philosophical Foundation: Liberty, Autonomy, and Moral Pluralism

1. Liberty as the Core of Free Speech

Liberal political theory holds that individuals possess a basic right to self‑determination: the freedom to form, revise, and pursue their own conceptions of the good life, provided they do not infringe on the equal liberty of others. When the state bans or restricts certain kinds of expression, it effectively substitutes a collective moral judgment for the private judgments of its citizens. Modern pluralistic societies accept that reasonable people can—and do—disagree about what constitutes moral or obscene material. Moral pluralism does not require that all moral viewpoints be given legal backing; rather, it demands that the law remain neutral on contested questions of value. A law that criminalizes “obscene” material imposes one particular moral stance, thereby marginalizing those who do not share it. In a free society, the existence of diverse sexual tastes and artistic representations is a natural consequence of moral diversity, not a danger to be eradicated.

John Stuart Mill’s harm principle asserts that the only justification for interfering with an individual’s liberty is to prevent harm to others. Purely self‑regarding behavior—behavior that does not directly cause non‑consensual harm—falls outside the scope of legitimate state action. Most pornography, as a consensual product of adult creators and consumers, does not meet the threshold of “harm to others” that would justify legal restriction. Obscenity statutes are inherently content‑based: they criminalize speech because of its subject matter. International instruments such as the International Covenant on Civil and Political Rights (ICCPR) protect the right to freedom of expression, but they also recognize that restrictions must be “provided by law” and “necessary … for the respect of the rights or reputations of others.” The United Nations Human Rights Committee has consistently interpreted “necessary” to require a high threshold of justification. blanket bans on pornographic material do not meet this threshold because they are overly broad and fail to demonstrate a direct, proportionate link to the protection of any legitimate right. The case for complete deregulation of pornography rests on the bedrock principles of liberty, pluralism, and the limited scope of legitimate state power. In a free society, competent adults must retain the right to make their own choices about what media to consume, create, and distribute. The Case for Complete Deregulation of Pornography: An Absolutist Free Speech Argument

Introduction

The regulation of pornographic content by the state represents one of the most enduring and philosophically untenable intrusions on individual liberty in modern democratic societies. From the Comstock laws of the nineteenth century to contemporary obscenity statutes, governments have persistently claimed the authority to dictate what consenting adults may create, distribute, and consume in their private lives. This essay argues that all obscenity laws and government restrictions on pornographic content involving consenting adults should be abolished, grounded in principles of absolute free expression, individual autonomy, and the demonstrable failures and inherent contradictions of censorship regimes.

This argument applies strictly to content involving consenting adults. The legal prohibitions surrounding the exploitation of minors are grounded not in obscenity doctrine but in the prevention of direct, documentable harm to individuals incapable of consent—a categorically different legal and moral framework that this essay does not challenge.

I. The Philosophical Foundation: Speech is Speech

The most fundamental argument against obscenity law is deceptively simple: expression does not cease to be expression merely because it is sexual. The First Amendment to the United States Constitution, and analogous provisions in democratic constitutions worldwide, protect the freedom of expression not because expression is always pleasant, enlightening, or morally uplifting, but because the alternative—granting the government the power to determine which ideas, images, and forms of communication are permissible—is incompatible with a free society.

Justice Hugo Black articulated the absolutist position with characteristic clarity: "No law means no law." When the First Amendment declares that Congress shall make no law abridging the freedom of speech or of the press, it does not append an asterisk directing readers to exceptions for content deemed vulgar, arousing, or offensive. The text is unequivocal.

Yet obscenity doctrine carves out precisely such an exception. In Roth v. United States (1957), the Supreme Court declared that obscenity falls outside the protection of the First Amendment entirely, a position reaffirmed and elaborated in Miller v. California (1973). The Miller test asks whether the average person, applying contemporary community standards, would find that a work, taken as a whole, appeals to the prurient interest; whether the work depicts sexual conduct in a patently offensive way; and whether the work, taken as a whole, lacks serious literary, artistic, political, or scientific value.

Each prong of this test is a philosophical catastrophe. The notion that expression can be stripped of constitutional protection because it appeals to "prurient interest" presupposes that sexual desire is inherently degrading or dangerous—a puritanical assumption masquerading as legal reasoning. The "patently offensive" standard delegates constitutional rights to the sensibilities of the majority, precisely the tyranny the Bill of Rights was designed to prevent. And the requirement of "serious value" transforms judges and jurors into art critics, empowered to decide which forms of human expression possess sufficient merit to deserve protection.

As Justice William Brennan—who authored the Roth decision—later acknowledged in his dissent in Paris Adult Theatre I v. Slaton (1973), the obscenity doctrine had proven irredeemably unworkable. After sixteen years of attempting to define obscenity, Brennan conceded that the task was inherently impossible without infringing on protected speech. If the author of modern obscenity doctrine himself ultimately recognized its futility, the continued insistence on maintaining it reflects institutional inertia rather than constitutional principle.

II. The Autonomy Argument

At the heart of the case for deregulation lies the principle of individual autonomy. In a liberal democratic society, the default position must be that competent adults are sovereign over their own bodies, minds, and choices. The burden of justification falls not on the individual who wishes to create or consume sexually explicit material, but on the state that seeks to prevent them from doing so.

John Stuart Mill's harm principle provides the essential framework: "The only purpose for which power can be rightfully exercised over any member of a civilized community, against his will, is to prevent harm to others." Obscenity laws fail this test decisively. When consenting adults produce, distribute, and consume pornographic material, the chain of voluntary choice is unbroken. No one is compelled to participate in its creation, and no one is forced to view it. The offense experienced by those who disapprove of its existence is real but legally irrelevant—the harm principle does not encompass the displeasure one feels at knowing others are engaged in activities one finds distasteful.

The autonomy argument extends to sexual expression specifically because sexuality is among the most intimate and personal dimensions of human life. If the state may not (in most modern democracies) regulate consensual sexual conduct between adults—a principle affirmed in Lawrence v. Texas (2003)—then the logical extension is that it may not regulate the depiction of such conduct. The distinction between doing and depicting collapses under scrutiny: if the act is legal, criminalizing its representation amounts to punishing communication about lawful behavior.

Furthermore, the autonomy principle encompasses both consumers and creators. Pornographic performers who freely choose their profession exercise agency over their own bodies. Treating them as incapable of genuine consent—as paternalistic regulatory frameworks implicitly do—infantilizes adults and denies their capacity for self-determination. This paternalism disproportionately affects women, paradoxically replicating the very power dynamics that some proponents of regulation claim to oppose.

III. The Empirical Argument: Regulation Does Not Achieve Its Stated Goals

Proponents of obscenity laws typically advance two empirical claims: that pornography causes measurable social harm, and that legal restrictions effectively reduce those harms. Both claims are, at best, poorly supported.

The social science literature on pornography's effects is vast, contradictory, and plagued by methodological limitations. While some studies suggest correlations between pornography consumption and various negative outcomes—such as distorted sexual expectations or relationship dissatisfaction—correlation is not causation, and the research is far from conclusive. Other studies have found no significant negative effects, and some have identified potential benefits, including reduced rates of sexual violence.

The work of Milton Diamond, a researcher at the University of Hawaii, has been particularly instructive. Countries such as Denmark, which effectively legalized pornography in 1969, saw decreases in reported sex crimes following liberalization. Japan, with its extraordinarily permissive pornography market, maintains sexual assault rates dramatically lower than those of more restrictive Western nations.

This does not establish that pornography prevents sexual violence—such a causal claim would suffer from the same methodological weaknesses that plague claims of harm. Even if one grants arguendo that some pornographic content produces negative social effects, this does not justify censorship within a consistent free speech framework. Political speech can radicalize. Religious speech can inspire intolerance. Commercial speech can promote unhealthy consumption. We do not censor these categories of speech because of their potential negative effects; we address the effects through education, counter-speech, and targeted regulation of conduct rather than expression. Sexual speech deserves no less.

What offends in one community may be unremarkable in another. The history of obscenity law is a chronicle of suppression directed at marginalized communities, dissenting voices, and cultural innovators. The Comstock Act of 1873 was used not only against pornography but against information about contraception and reproductive health. Margaret Sanger was indicted under federal obscenity statutes for distributing pamphlets about birth control. The law was wielded against early advocates of homosexual rights, effectively criminalizing public discussion of same-sex desire.

Homophile organizations were prosecuted for distributing material that would have been unremarkable if the subjects depicted had been heterosexual. The obscenity framework provided a veneer of content-neutral respectability for what was, in practice, systematic persecution of sexual minorities.

This history is not merely antiquarian. It reveals the structural tendency of obscenity law to target the vulnerable and the unconventional while leaving the powerful and the mainstream undisturbed. A legal tool that has been so consistently abused cannot be reformed; it must be abolished.

The feminist argument against pornography, articulated most powerfully by Catharine MacKinnon and Andrea Dworkin in the 1980s, deserves serious engagement. MacKinnon and Dworkin argued that pornography is not speech but a practice of sex discrimination, that it subordinates women and constitutes a violation of their civil rights. First, it depends on treating a category of expression as equivalent to conduct—a conflation that, if accepted, would undermine the very concept of protected speech.
